title: Ionic and covalent bonding, Lewis structures
note: Metals give electrons to nonmetals to form ions held by electrostatic attraction (ionic bonds); nonmetals share electron pairs (covalent bonds). In a Lewis structure, count valence electrons, connect atoms with single bonds, complete octets on outer atoms, then use multiple bonds if the central atom is short. Formal charge = valence − lone-pair electrons − ½ bonding electrons.

read.title: Giving electrons and sharing them
text: Atoms bond because the bonded arrangement has lower energy than the separate atoms. There are two main ways this happens. When a metal meets a nonmetal, the metal tends to lose electrons and the nonmetal tends to gain them. Sodium becomes Na⁺ and chlorine becomes Cl⁻, and the ions attract each other in a rigid crystal. Ionic solids have high melting points and conduct electricity only when melted or dissolved, because only then can their ions move.

When two nonmetals meet, neither gives up electrons easily, so they share pairs instead. A shared pair is a covalent bond. If the two atoms differ in electronegativity, the pair is pulled toward one side and the bond is polar. Two or three shared pairs make double and triple bonds, which are shorter and stronger than single bonds between the same atoms.

Lewis structures track the valence electrons. Count them, adding one for each negative charge and removing one for each positive charge. Join the atoms with single bonds, usually around the least electronegative atom, and complete the octets of the outer atoms. Put leftover electrons on the central atom. If it is still short of eight, turn lone pairs into multiple bonds. When several valid structures exist, formal charges help choose the best one, and resonance describes molecules that no single drawing captures.
